extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of logic; logicians and philosophers studying methods of inference
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, procedures, and evaluative criteria for applying the Indirect Method of Inference (logical alphabet/abacus/machine) to deduce, test, and analyse propositions; includes how to represent propositions mechanically and how to detect fallacy, equivalence, consistency, and contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Negative-premise and Undistributed-middle fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indirect Method of Inference prevents drawing fallacious conclusions that arise from negative premises or from an undistributed middle term in traditional syllogisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the text shows how premises that assert negatives or leave middle terms undistributed fail to yield information (e.g. statements about basalt/granite and sedimentary rocks). Use the Indirect Method to reveal when premises give no information on a point rather than permitting a fallacious conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illicit process of the major term avoided by proper method
rubrics_metrics.description: When the rules of the Indirect Method are followed, the fallacy called the Illicit Process of the Major Term cannot be committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: premises 'All planets are subject to gravity' and 'Fixed stars are not planets' yield no valid conclusion that 'fixed stars are not subject to gravity.' Use the method's combination-analysis to show no conclusion about the connection between fixed stars and gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine all relevant combinations of the logical alphabet
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference requires checking the conceivable combinations of the logical alphabet corresponding to the terms in the premises (e.g. 2^n combinations for n terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges practical difficulty: number of combinations may be large, increasing labour and chance of mistake. Recommended mitigation: use mechanical aids (abacus or machine) or systematic modes to facilitate work; do not skip combinations when determining what premises imply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical representation and manipulation (Logical Abacus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent combinations as movable elements (pins/slips) and simulate class separation operations mechanically: raising/lowering/selecting combinations to reflect 'is' and 'is not' relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: mark combinations, use raised/lowered pins to separate those inconsistent with a premise, repeatedly select classes (A, B, a, b, etc.) to produce the remaining consistent combinations. Use this to divide combinations into those inconsistent with premises and those consistent, from which conclusions are read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of disjunctive propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disjunctive premises (A is either B or C or D) require more intricate selection steps so as not to reject combinations that the disjunction allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For 'A is B or C or D' together with 'A is not C and not D' the correct procedure selectively rejects only inconsistent combinations (iteratively select and deselect within the A's to leave AB as the sole A). Do not treat disjunctions like simple exclusives; preserve permitted alternatives until contradictions eliminate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine operation: press keys in sequence matching symbolic notation
rubrics_metrics.description: To use the Logical Machine, reduce premises to the simple symbolic notation used (letters and operation keys) and press the corresponding keys in succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For A = AB press A (left), copula, A (right), B (right), full stop. After entering all premises, the machine displays the combinations consistent with those premises. Read conclusions from the remaining combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of operation keys: copula, disjunction, full-stop, and Finis
rubrics_metrics.description: Operation keys correspond to grammatical/marker functions: copula (is/=), disjunction (+/.|.), full stop (end of proposition), and Finis (restore machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full-stop finalizes a proposition and allows reading of current state; Finis restores the machine to show all conceivable combinations (initial condition) before starting a new problem. Use these keys appropriately to control the machine's internal state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double (transposed) reading rule for identities
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple identity must be entered in double form: read each proposition as it stands and play the keys, then convert (transpose) the proposition and play the keys again in the transposed order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper rule: (1) Read each proposition and play corresponding keys. (2) Convert the proposition and play keys again in transposed order of terms. Examples requiring this include A = B, AB = CD, AB = AC, etc. Exception: for some partial identities the second (transposed) reading may have no effect and can be omitted after experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent simple identities as two partial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine cannot accept a simple identity A = B except by entering the double form A = B and B = A (i.e., representing identity as two partial identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for encoding: always include both directions when encoding identities unless the form is a partial identity known to be stable under single reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect self-contradiction by disappearance of letter-terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine (or abacus) will detect self-contradiction: if premises are self-contradictory, one or more letter-terms will disappear entirely from the Logical Alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: after entering premises, if a letter (or its negative) wholly disappears from the set of remaining combinations, infer that some act of self-contradiction has been committed (e.g., entering both 'A is B' and 'A is not B' leads to no combinations containing A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency criterion: each term and its negative must remain somewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Two (or more) propositions are consistent provided that, after striking out combinations inconsistent with them, each term and the negative of each term still appears somewhere in the remaining Logical Alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If after eliminating inconsistent combinations all letters A, a, B, b, etc., remain present somewhere, then no inconsistency exists, even if propositions are not equivalent or inferrible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of premises is logically indifferent
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical order in which premises are stated has no effect on the logical result (the combinations of the logical alphabet are the same regardless of statement order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although convenience or ease of human inference may vary with order (easier to gather conclusions from some orders), do not treat premise order as significant for logical validity when using the Indirect Method or the machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations between propositions: equivalent, inferrible, consistent, contradictory
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify relation of any proposition/group to another as one of four: Equivalent (mutual inference), Inferrible (one removes some but not all combinations the other removes), Consistent (jointly allow each term and its negative to remain), or Contradictory (together remove one or more letter-terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test of equivalence: capability of mutual inference (each can be derived from the other). Equivalence can be operationalised as 'remove the same combinations from the Logical Alphabet.' Use the logical alphabet/machine to test these relations by comparing removed combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure import of a statement by the combinations it destroys
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning (import) of a proposition is measured by which combinations of terms it excludes from the Logical Alphabet; propositions are equivalent when they remove the same combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical use: to determine whether one proposition contains the whole information of another, compare the sets of combinations each removes. This gives a precise, mechanical criterion for inferibility and equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference only explicates implicit content; no new implicit knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference (deductive or inductive) cannot add new implicit knowledge beyond what is contained in the premises; it only explicates or unfolds information already implicit in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an argument, check that the conclusion is implicit in the premises. Beware claims that inference creates genuinely new content; novelty-seeking (finding equivalents not obvious) is an inverse, inductive task and may be tentative and laborious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting logical equivalents is laborious and not infallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the combinations consistent with premises can be re-expressed as an equivalent proposition, finding all alternative equivalent forms is difficult and may have no uniform infallible process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical warning: do not assume you have found all equivalents; discovery often requires repeated trial. The task resembles induction (inverse of deduction) and may be uncertain in complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical aids are pedagogically and demonstratively useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical abacus/machine are valuable chiefly for (1) teaching — to exhibit clear visible analysis of logical problems step-by-step, and (2) demonstrating the correctness/general character of the Indirect Method (e.g., Boole's results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: mechanical devices may not have wide practical utility in everyday life, but they reduce human error and make steps explicit. Use them when complexity or pedagogical clarity demands, but expect some mental labour in interpretation and gathering conclusions.
